title: Treatment Evidence Map
description: Interactive card-sorting activity. Learners sort 13 gut-brain treatments (fecal microbiota transplant and microbiome products, implanted and noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation, consumer wellness gadgets, low-dose tricyclic antidepressants, and biologics) into approved, cleared, or standard care; experimental; or unproven or unsafe. Immediate feedback gives the FDA status as of October 2026 and the evidence behind each answer.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Classify gut-brain treatments by FDA status and strength of evidence: approved, cleared, or standard care; experimental; or unproven or unsafe.
Explain why approval for one condition does not mean approval for another, using vagus nerve stimulation and fecal microbiota products as examples.
Justify each classification with the type and size of the supporting evidence.
prerequisites: The vagus nerve as a two-way gut-brain pathway (Chapter 2)
Dysbiosis and antibiotic disruption of the microbiome (Chapter 3)
How supplements are regulated differently from medicines (Chapter 16)
keyQuestions: What exactly is each vagus nerve stimulator approved, cleared, or authorized for?
Why is FMT standard care for recurrent C. difficile but experimental for other conditions?
How can an off-label treatment still count as standard care?
What makes a consumer wellness gadget different from a medical device?
misconceptions: A treatment approved for one condition is approved for related conditions.
Natural treatments such as stool transplants are automatically safe.
A device that is cleared or authorized is the same as one that is approved.
Prescribing an antidepressant for IBS means the doctor thinks symptoms are imaginary.
